papers.t: General Introduction
papers.s: Hamilton opens the series: Americans must decide whether good government can come from reflection and choice, and he lists the topics to come.
papers.c: The Constitutional Convention had finished in September 1787. New York's ratifying convention would meet the next summer, and the state's popular governor, George Clinton, was against the plan. Newspapers were full of letters for and against it, including the Anti-Federalist "Cato" and "Brutus" essays. Hamilton began this series to answer them.
papers.m: Hamilton says the choice before New York may decide whether any people can set up a government on purpose, by thinking it through, instead of by accident or force. He admits that both sides include honest people and that self-interest can cloud judgment on either side. He asks readers to weigh the plan on its merits, then lays out six topics the series will cover.
qs: What does Hamilton mean by government from "reflection and choice" as opposed to "accident and force"?
Hamilton admits that wise and good men are found on both sides. Why might a writer arguing for one side say this?
Look at the six topics he promises. Which ones does the series spend the most time on, judging by the groups on the guide page?

k.q: whether societies of men are really capable or not of establishing good government from reflection and choice
k.w: The most quoted sentence in the series: the stakes are bigger than one state.

k.q: a dangerous ambition more often lurks behind the specious mask of zeal for the rights of the people
k.w: Hamilton warns that loud talk about liberty can hide ambition. Anti-Federalists said the same of the Constitution's backers.

k.q: I propose, in a series of papers, to discuss the following interesting particulars
k.w: The plan of the whole work. Compare it with what the series actually covers.

papers.t: Concerning Dangers from Foreign Force and Influence
papers.s: Jay argues that Americans are one people and that a strong Union will protect them from foreign powers.
papers.c: John Jay was New York's leading diplomat and the Confederation's Secretary for Foreign Affairs. He wrote the first essays after Hamilton's introduction, on the danger of foreign influence and war.
papers.m: Jay says that some writers now suggest splitting the country into several confederacies. He answers that Americans share one connected land, the same language and, he says, the same religion, and they fought one war for independence together. The people chose union from the start; the Convention was made up of trusted men; its plan deserves a calm and fair hearing.
qs: Jay says Americans are "one united people." What evidence does he give? What might a critic add or question?
Why does Jay bring up the idea of several separate confederacies? Who was suggesting it?
Jay says the plan is "recommended, not imposed." Why does that matter to his argument?

k.q: Nothing is more certain than the indispensable necessity of government
k.w: Jay's starting point: people must give up some natural rights to any government.

k.q: Providence has been pleased to give this one connected country to one united people
k.w: Jay's picture of a single American people. Notice who is left out of his description; the country was more varied than he says.

k.q: This convention composed of men who possessed the confidence of the people
k.w: He asks readers to trust the Convention's members, an appeal to reputation that Anti-Federalists said should not replace examining the plan.

papers.t: The Same Subject Continued (Concerning Dangers From Foreign Force and Influence)
papers.s: Jay argues that one national government will give foreign nations fewer just causes for war, because it will keep treaties and the law of nations more faithfully than thirteen states.
papers.c: In the 1780s states sometimes ignored the 1783 peace treaty with Britain, for example on debts owed to British merchants. Britain used this as a reason to keep forts on American soil.
papers.m: Jay says wars come from just causes, like broken treaties or violence, and from pretended ones. A national government will choose abler officials, read treaties the same way everywhere, and be less tempted by the interests of one state. It can also settle disputes calmly, because a strong nation's apologies are accepted when a weak state's are not.
qs: What is the difference between a "just" cause of war and a pretended one, in Jay's terms?
Why does Jay think a national government would pick better officials than the states?
Can you think of a reason a state government might handle a border problem better than a distant national one?

k.q: that of providing for their SAFETY seems to be the first
k.w: Safety is the first object of government, and it frames Nos. 3 to 5.

k.q: treaties and articles of treaties, as well as the laws of nations, will always be expounded in one sense
k.w: An argument for one national court system, which Hamilton takes up later in No. 80.

k.q: In the year 1685, the state of Genoa having offended Louis XIV.
k.w: Jay's story of a weak state forced to humble itself before a strong king.

papers.t: The Same Subject Continued (Concerning Dangers From Foreign Force and Influence)
papers.s: Jay continues: foreign nations will look for pretended causes of war, and only a united America can deter them.
papers.c: Spain had closed the lower Mississippi River to American trade, and Britain kept American ships out of its West Indies trade. These were live disputes in 1787.
papers.m: Jay says nations often go to war for gain, pride or rivalry, not only for good reasons. America competed with Britain and France in fishing and shipping and with others in the China trade. One government can draw on the whole country's talent, money and men, and command a single navy and militia. Divided states would be easy prey.
qs: List the trade rivalries Jay names. Why would they make other nations unfriendly?
How does Jay use the example of Great Britain's union?
Jay says foreign nations will treat us according to how we are governed. What does he mean?

k.q: nations in general will make war whenever they have a prospect of getting anything by it
k.w: Jay's plain view of how nations behave.

k.q: Spain thinks it convenient to shut the Mississippi against us
k.w: A real grievance in 1787, especially for people living west of the mountains.

k.q: What would the militia of Britain be if the English militia obeyed the government of England
k.w: His comparison with Britain's union of England and Scotland.

papers.t: The Same Subject Continued (Concerning Dangers From Foreign Force and Influence)
papers.s: Jay finishes the foreign-danger papers: separate American confederacies would become rivals, as England, Scotland and Wales once were, and foreign powers would play them off against each other.
papers.c: Jay opens with Queen Anne's 1706 letter urging the union of England and Scotland, which took place in 1707.
papers.m: Jay argues that three or four American confederacies would not stay equal. One would grow stronger, and the others would fear and envy it. Each might seek foreign allies against its neighbors. So disunion would invite the very foreign meddling that union prevents.
qs: Why does Jay think separate confederacies could not stay on equal terms?
How would foreign nations take advantage of a divided America, in Jay's view?
Is the British example a good fit for America? Explain.

k.q: QUEEN ANNE, in her letter of the 1st July, 1706
k.w: Jay borrows a British example of union bringing peace.

k.q: The North is generally the region of strength
k.w: Jay imagines a northern confederacy outgrowing the others.

k.q: Let candid men judge
k.w: His closing appeal.

papers.t: Concerning Dangers from Dissensions Between the States
papers.s: Hamilton argues that if the states split apart they would go to war with one another, because nations and their leaders are moved by ambition, rivalry and passion, and trade does not end wars.
papers.c: Shays's Rebellion in Massachusetts (1786–1787) was fresh in readers' minds, and Hamilton mentions it. Some writers of the day argued that trading republics are naturally peaceful.
papers.m: Hamilton lists the causes of war: love of power, rivalry, and the private passions of leaders. He gives examples from Athens to Britain. He rejects the idea that commerce makes republics peaceful: Sparta, Athens, Rome, Carthage, Venice, Holland and Britain all went to war often. Neighboring nations, he says, are natural enemies unless joined in a common government.
qs: Why does Hamilton list so many examples from history? Do they prove his point?
What is Hamilton's answer to people who say trading republics are peaceful?
Hamilton mentions Shays's Rebellion. How does it fit his argument?

k.q: A man must be far gone in Utopian speculations
k.w: Hamilton's blunt opening claim.

k.q: Has commerce hitherto done anything more than change the objects of war?
k.w: His answer to those who said trade brings peace.

k.q: NEIGHBORING nations (says he) are naturally enemies of each other
k.w: Hamilton quotes a French writer (the Abbé de Mably) to support his case.

papers.t: The Same Subject Continued (Concerning Dangers from Dissensions Between the States)
papers.s: Hamilton names the likely causes of war between separate states: western lands, trade rules, the public debt, laws breaking private contracts, and rival foreign alliances.
papers.c: Several states claimed land west of the Appalachians, and Connecticut and Pennsylvania had clashed over the Wyoming Valley. New York and Vermont had quarreled too.
papers.m: Hamilton shows how specific disputes could turn into armed conflict without a common umpire. States fighting over western land, taxing each other's trade, arguing over shares of the war debt, or allying with different foreign powers would have no court and no government above them to keep the peace.
qs: Which of the causes Hamilton lists do you think was most dangerous? Why?
What does an "umpire or common judge" have to do with keeping peace between states?
How did the Constitution's courts later settle disputes between states?

k.q: Territorial disputes have at all times been found one of the most fertile sources of hostility
k.w: The first and largest cause he names.

k.q: without any umpire or common judge to interpose
k.w: The key idea: disputes need a referee.

k.q: The public debt of the Union would be a further cause of collision
k.w: A money quarrel that would come back in the 1790s debate over the debt.

papers.t: The Consequences of Hostilities Between the States
papers.s: Hamilton warns that war among the states would bring standing armies, stronger executives and less liberty, while a Union, like Britain's island position, makes large armies unneeded.
papers.c: Americans of the time feared standing armies, remembering British troops in Boston before the Revolution. Anti-Federalists warned that the Constitution would allow a permanent army.
papers.m: Hamilton turns the fear of armies around. Separate states bordering each other would build forts and armies for safety, and war would make the military powerful and liberty weak. A united country, protected by an ocean, can keep a small army and rely on a navy, as Britain does.
qs: How does Hamilton use the fear of standing armies to argue for the Union?
Why does an island nation need a smaller army, in Hamilton's view?
Read an Anti-Federalist essay on standing armies. How would its author answer Hamilton?

k.q: Safety from external danger is the most powerful director of national conduct
k.w: Fear, he says, leads even free nations to give up liberty.

k.q: STANDING ARMIES and the correspondent appendages of military establishments
k.w: He names the institutions everyone feared.

k.q: If we are wise enough to preserve the Union we may for ages enjoy an advantage similar to that of an insulated situation
k.w: His central comparison with Britain.

papers.t: The Union as a Safeguard Against Domestic Faction and Insurrection
papers.s: Hamilton argues that a confederate republic guards against faction and rebellion, and he uses Montesquieu, the favorite authority of the Constitution's opponents, to make his case.
papers.c: Anti-Federalists often cited the French writer Montesquieu, who said republics must be small. Hamilton answers by quoting Montesquieu's praise of confederate republics.
papers.m: Hamilton admits that the small republics of Greece and Italy were torn by disorder. But political science has improved: separation of powers, checks and balances, independent judges, and elected representatives are new tools. A confederate republic, made of smaller states, can stop a revolt in one part with the strength of the rest. The Constitution, he says, keeps the states as parts of the national government.
qs: What "improvements" in the science of politics does Hamilton list? Which ones are in the Constitution?
Why does Hamilton quote Montesquieu at length?
Anti-Federalists said the plan was a "consolidation." How does Hamilton answer?

k.q: The science of politics, however, like most other sciences, has received great improvement
k.w: His list of new inventions in government, which reads like a summary of the Constitution.

k.q: CONFEDERATE REPUBLIC
k.w: Montesquieu's term. Hamilton uses it to show that a large federal republic can work.

k.q: A distinction, more subtle than accurate, has been raised between a CONFEDERACY and a CONSOLIDATION
k.w: He dismisses a distinction that was central to the Anti-Federalist case.

papers.t: The Same Subject Continued (The Union as a Safeguard Against Domestic Faction and Insurrection)
papers.s: Madison's most famous paper: faction cannot be removed without destroying liberty, but a large republic with representatives can control its effects.
papers.c: Madison had studied failed republics before the Convention and had seen state legislatures pass laws he thought unjust, such as paper-money and debt-relief laws. Anti-Federalists, citing Montesquieu, argued that republics had to be small. This was Madison's first Federalist paper.
papers.m: Madison defines a faction as any group, majority or minority, moved by an interest or passion against others' rights or the common good. Its causes are "sown in the nature of man," above all unequal property. You cannot remove the causes without removing liberty, so you must control the effects. A small democracy cannot do that, because a majority faction can easily take over. A large republic can: representatives filter public views, and a wide country contains so many interests that no single majority faction is likely to form.
qs: What are the two ways of curing faction, and why does Madison reject one of them?
Why does Madison think a large republic is safer from majority faction than a small one? Do you find this convincing?
Brutus I argued the opposite: that a free republic cannot work over a large territory. Compare the two arguments.
Many readers today see political parties as factions. Would Madison? Use his definition.

k.q: By a faction, I understand a number of citizens
k.w: Madison's definition. Note that a faction can be a majority.

k.q: Liberty is to faction what air is to fire
k.w: Why the cure of removing liberty is worse than the disease.

k.q: the most common and durable source of factions has been the various and unequal distribution of property
k.w: Madison names economic interest as the main source of division.

k.q: Enlightened statesmen will not always be at the helm
k.w: Why good leaders cannot be the whole answer.

k.q: Extend the sphere, and you take in a greater variety of parties and interests
k.w: The heart of the extended-republic argument.

papers.t: The Utility of the Union in Respect to Commercial Relations and a Navy
papers.s: Hamilton argues that a Union can bargain with Europe over trade, build a navy, protect the fisheries and river rights, and create "one great American system."
papers.c: After independence Britain closed much of its trade to American ships, and the states, each making its own trade laws, could not answer together.
papers.m: Hamilton says a united country could use its market to force fair trade terms from Europe, and could build a navy that would make it a power worth courting. Divided, the states would undercut one another and foreign nations would set the terms. He closes by urging Americans to stand up to European claims of superiority.
qs: Why can thirteen states with separate trade laws not bargain well with Britain?
What would a navy do for the country, according to Hamilton?
Hamilton's ending answers European writers who claimed America made animals and people "degenerate." Why include this in an argument about trade?

k.q: By prohibitory regulations, extending, at the same time, throughout the States
k.w: The power of a single trade policy.

k.q: A further resource for influencing the conduct of European nations toward us
k.w: His case for a federal navy.

k.q: Let the thirteen States, bound together in a strict and indissoluble Union, concur in erecting one great American system
k.w: The famous ending, written to stir pride.

papers.t: The Utility of the Union In Respect to Revenue
papers.s: Hamilton argues that one national government could collect far more revenue from import duties, with less smuggling, than separate states could.
papers.c: Under the Articles of Confederation, Congress could not tax. It asked the states for money, and the states often paid little or nothing. A proposal to let Congress collect an import duty had failed because one state's consent was missing.
papers.m: Hamilton says commerce is the main source of national wealth and of the ability to pay taxes. In America, import duties will be the main tax for a long time, because people dislike excise taxes and land is hard to tax. Separate states, with long land borders between them, could not stop smuggling; one nation would have only the Atlantic coast to guard.
qs: Why does Hamilton think import duties will be the main source of federal revenue?
How would separate states make smuggling easier?
Brutus warned that Congress's taxing power would leave the states nothing. How might Hamilton answer?

k.q: The prosperity of commerce is now perceived and acknowledged by all enlightened statesmen
k.w: The opening claim about trade and wealth.

k.q: there will be, as to the principal part of our commerce, but ONE SIDE to guard
k.w: His argument from geography.

k.q: A nation cannot long exist without revenues
k.w: The stakes, in one sentence.

papers.t: Advantage of the Union in Respect to Economy in Government
papers.s: Hamilton argues that one national government would cost less than the several governments that would be needed if the states split into confederacies.
papers.c: Some opponents feared the new government would be expensive. Hamilton answers with the opposite claim. This is one of the shortest papers.
papers.m: Hamilton says any separate confederacy would need a government nearly as large as the one proposed. Several of them would cost more than one, plus guards along their borders to stop smuggling. Thirteen states can support one government more easily than any smaller group can.
qs: Why would separate confederacies need governments nearly as large as the national one?
Is cost a strong argument for or against a form of government? What else matters?

k.q: The money saved from one object may be usefully applied to another
k.w: His opening point about economy.

k.q: Nothing can be more evident than that the thirteen States will be able to support a national government better
k.w: The core claim.

papers.t: Objections to the Proposed Constitution From Extent of Territory Answered
papers.s: Madison answers the objection that the country is too large for a republic: a republic, unlike a direct democracy, can extend over a wide area because representatives meet for the people.
papers.c: This paper finishes the argument begun in No. 10. Madison also describes the size of the country under the 1783 treaty and looks ahead to roads and canals.
papers.m: Madison says the error comes from confusing a democracy, where citizens meet in person, with a republic, where representatives meet. A republic's natural limit is the distance representatives can travel to meet, and the United States is within it. The national government has only certain listed powers; the states keep the rest. New roads and canals will bring the country closer. He ends by urging Americans not to give up their union and their bold experiment.
qs: What is the difference between a democracy and a republic in Madison's sense?
How does Madison use the actual size of the country to make his point?
Cato III argued the country was too large for one government. Whose argument is stronger, and why?

k.q: in a democracy, the people meet and exercise the government in person
k.w: Madison's key distinction.

k.q: Its jurisdiction is limited to certain enumerated objects
k.w: He reassures readers that the states keep most powers.

k.q: Hearken not to the unnatural voice
k.w: His warm closing appeal.

k.q: Is it not the glory of the people of America
k.w: He praises Americans for not following ancient custom blindly.

papers.t: The Insufficiency of the Present Confederation to Preserve the Union
papers.s: Hamilton names the great flaw of the Articles: Congress makes rules for states, not for individuals, so it cannot enforce its own laws.
papers.c: Under the Articles of Confederation (in force since 1781), Congress could ask the states for money and troops but could not make them comply. By 1787 many states paid little of what Congress requested, and the country could not pay its war debts.
papers.m: Hamilton describes "the last stage of national humiliation": unpaid debts, foreign territory held on American soil, no credit, no trade policy. The root problem is "legislation for states" in their collective capacity. A law needs a penalty; against a state, the only penalty is force, which means war. A real government must act directly on individuals, through courts and officers.
qs: What does Hamilton mean by "legislation for states" as opposed to legislation for individuals?
Why does he think a law against a whole state can only be enforced by war?
Do Anti-Federalists agree that the Articles needed fixing? Read Federal Farmer I and compare.

k.q: We may indeed with propriety be said to have reached almost the last stage of national humiliation
k.w: His list of the country's troubles follows.

k.q: The great and radical vice in the construction of the existing Confederation
k.w: The core diagnosis of Nos. 15 to 22.

k.q: Why has government been instituted at all?
k.w: A famous line about human nature and the need for law.

papers.t: The Same Subject Continued (The Insufficiency of the Present Confederation to Preserve the Union)
papers.s: Hamilton argues that coercing states by force would mean civil war, so the national government must have its own courts and officers to enforce laws on individuals.
papers.c: Hamilton continues No. 15, with examples from European confederacies.
papers.m: Using force against a disobedient state would split the Union, because other states would take sides. Instead, the new government will carry its laws to each citizen, with its own officers and courts. If a state legislature tried to block a federal law, it would have to act openly, and the courts and the people would judge it.
qs: Why would forcing a state to obey lead to war, in Hamilton's view?
What is the difference between a state's "non-compliance" and "active resistance"?
How does this paper prepare the ground for a national court system?

k.q: the parent of anarchy
k.w: Hamilton's name for the principle of legislating for states.

k.q: The plausibility of this objection will vanish the moment we advert to the essential difference between a mere NON-COMPLIANCE and a DIRECT and ACTIVE RESISTANCE
k.w: A key distinction about how states could resist.

k.q: If opposition to the national government should arise from the disorderly conduct of refractory or seditious individuals
k.w: How the new government would handle rebellion.

papers.t: The Same Subject Continued (The Insufficiency of the Present Confederation to Preserve the Union)
papers.s: Hamilton answers the fear that the national government will swallow the states: people's loyalty runs first to the governments closest to them.
papers.c: Anti-Federalists warned that the states would be absorbed into one national government. Hamilton argues the danger runs the other way.
papers.m: Hamilton says ambitious national leaders would have little reason to want the states' local business. And people feel more attached to their state, which handles their courts, property and daily life. So the states are more likely to encroach on the nation than the reverse. He points to medieval kingdoms, where powerful lords often defied weak kings.
qs: Why does Hamilton think people will stay more loyal to their states?
What is the "transcendant advantage" of the states?
In later history, has power moved toward the states or the national government? Give an example and say what changed.

k.q: It is a known fact in human nature, that its affections are commonly weak in proportion to the distance or diffusiveness of the object
k.w: The basic idea of the paper.

k.q: There is one transcendant advantage belonging to the province of the State governments
k.w: He means the everyday work of civil and criminal justice.

k.q: The separate governments in a confederacy may aptly be compared with the feudal baronies
k.w: His comparison with medieval Europe.

papers.t: The Same Subject Continued (The Insufficiency of the Present Confederation to Preserve the Union)
papers.s: Using ancient Greek leagues, the paper shows how confederacies with weak central councils fell into quarrels and foreign domination.
papers.c: Nos. 18 to 20 grew from notes Madison had made on ancient and modern confederacies before the Convention; Hamilton contributed some material. They review history to show that weak unions fail.
papers.m: The Amphictyonic council of Greece looked strong on paper but could not act against its members; the strong cities bullied the weak, and Philip of Macedon took advantage. The Achaean league was better organized and lasted longer, but it too was undone by division and outside powers.
qs: Why did the Amphictyonic council fail even though it had large powers on paper?
What made the Achaean league stronger? Why did it still fail?
How do these ancient examples relate to the Articles of Confederation?

k.q: In theory, and upon paper, this apparatus of powers seems amply sufficient
k.w: The gap between paper powers and real ones.

k.q: Very different, nevertheless, was the experiment from the theory
k.w: The lesson the authors draw.

k.q: The Achaean league, as it is called
k.w: The second, better example.

papers.t: The Same Subject Continued (The Insufficiency of the Present Confederation to Preserve the Union)
papers.s: The paper reviews the Holy Roman Empire, Poland and the Swiss cantons to show that confederacies of sovereign states are weak and quarrelsome.
papers.c: The authors continue their history lesson with examples from Europe in their own time.
papers.m: The German empire had an emperor and a diet with large powers, but its members fought each other and ignored its decisions. Poland was even worse. The Swiss cantons held together mainly because of their mountains, their weakness and their fear of neighbors, and even they had come to blows.
qs: Why do the authors say the German empire was weak despite its "parade of constitutional powers"?
Why is Switzerland not a good example for America, in their view?
Patrick Henry pointed to Switzerland as a model. Compare his view in his June 5 speech.

k.q: The history of Germany is a history of wars between the emperor and the princes and states
k.w: The main lesson from Germany.

k.q: The connection among the Swiss cantons scarcely amounts to a confederacy
k.w: Why Switzerland is not a good model.

k.q: They are kept together by the peculiarity of their topographical position
k.w: Geography, not government, keeps the Swiss together.

papers.t: The Same Subject Continued (The Insufficiency of the Present Confederation to Preserve the Union)
papers.s: The paper examines the Dutch republic: its union could not raise money or act without unanimous consent, and only a hereditary leader and fear of neighbors held it together.
papers.c: The United Netherlands were a well-known republic and trading power. In 1787 they were in political turmoil.
papers.m: The Dutch union's rules required unanimity and gave the central body no power to collect taxes. In emergencies it broke its own rules. The authors conclude that experience is the best teacher: a government over governments, legislating for states rather than individuals, does not work.
qs: Why did the Dutch union often break its own constitution?
What does "Experience is the oracle of truth" mean here?
After reading Nos. 18 to 20, what pattern do the authors see in failed confederacies?

k.q: Such is the nature of the celebrated Belgic confederacy, as delineated on parchment
k.w: Again, the gap between the written plan and real practice.

k.q: In critical emergencies, the States-General are often compelled to overleap their constitutional bounds
k.w: Weak rules lead to rule-breaking.

k.q: Experience is the oracle of truth
k.w: The conclusion of the history papers.

papers.t: Other Defects of the Present Confederation
papers.s: Hamilton lists more defects of the Articles: no power to enforce laws, no guarantee of state governments, and an unfair system of quotas for raising money.
papers.c: Shays's Rebellion had shown that the Confederation could not help a state put down an uprising.
papers.m: Congress has no means to punish disobedience. There is no guarantee that a state's republican government will be protected from rebellion. Money is raised by quotas based on land values, which cannot measure a state's real wealth and so are unjust. Taxes on what people buy are better, because they limit themselves: tax too much and people buy less.
qs: What does Hamilton mean by a "sanction"? Why does a law need one?
Why does Hamilton think quotas are unfair?
Why does Hamilton think consumption taxes cannot easily be pushed too high?

k.q: The next most palpable defect of the subsisting Confederation, is the total want of a SANCTION to its laws
k.w: No penalty, no law.

k.q: The want of a mutual guaranty of the State governments is another capital imperfection
k.w: Compare the Constitution's guarantee of a republican form of government (Article IV).

k.q: It is a signal advantage of taxes on articles of consumption, that they contain in their own nature a security against excess
k.w: His point about taxes that limit themselves.

papers.t: The Same Subject Continued (Other Defects of the Present Confederation)
papers.s: Hamilton finishes his list of the Articles' defects: no power over trade, a clumsy way to raise armies, equal votes for unequal states, no national courts, and a Congress that rests on the states rather than the people.
papers.c: This is the last paper of the group on the Articles. Hamilton closes with a principle that later appears in many debates: the national government must rest on the consent of the people.
papers.m: Hamilton says Congress cannot regulate commerce, so states fight trade wars with each other. Armies are raised by asking states, which is slow and unfair. Each state has one vote, so a small minority can block the majority, and the rule requiring nine states for big decisions makes deadlock worse. There are no national courts to give treaties and laws one meaning. And because the Articles were ratified by state legislatures, not the people, the Union's legal basis is weak.
qs: Why does Hamilton think requiring more than a majority can be harmful? Can you think of a reason to require a supermajority?
Why do laws need courts?
What does Hamilton mean by resting the government on "the consent of the people" rather than the states?

k.q: The want of a power to regulate commerce is by all parties allowed to be of the number
k.w: A point that even many Anti-Federalists granted.

k.q: what at first sight may seem a remedy, is, in reality, a poison
k.w: His case against supermajority rules.

k.q: Laws are a dead letter without courts to expound and define their true meaning and operation
k.w: A short case for a federal judiciary.

k.q: The fabric of American empire ought to rest on the solid basis of THE CONSENT OF THE PEOPLE
k.w: The paper's closing principle.

papers.t: The Necessity of a Government as Energetic as the One Proposed to the Preservation of the Union
papers.s: Hamilton begins the case for an energetic government: the powers for common defense must have no limits, because the dangers they meet cannot be foreseen.
papers.c: This starts the third topic Hamilton listed in No. 1: a government "at least equally energetic with the one proposed."
papers.m: The Union exists for common defense, peace at home, trade and foreign relations. For defense, the government must be able to raise armies, build fleets and pay for them, with no fixed limit, because "the circumstances that endanger the safety of nations are infinite." Whoever is responsible for an end must have the means. The real question is whether the government is built well enough to be trusted with such powers.
qs: Why does Hamilton think defense powers cannot be limited in advance?
What is the relationship between "means" and "ends" in his argument?
Anti-Federalists replied that unlimited powers invite abuse. How does Hamilton try to answer that worry at the end of the paper?

k.q: the circumstances that endanger the safety of nations are infinite
k.w: His central claim about defense powers.

k.q: the means ought to be proportioned to the end
k.w: A principle Hamilton returns to often.

k.q: Not to confer in each case a degree of power commensurate to the end, would be to violate the most obvious rules of prudence
k.w: Why limits on defense powers would be unwise.

papers.t: The Powers Necessary to the Common Defense Further Considered
papers.s: Hamilton answers the objection that the Constitution allows standing armies in peacetime, noting that most state constitutions and the Articles allowed them too.
papers.c: Many Anti-Federalists wanted a ban on peacetime armies. The Pennsylvania and North Carolina constitutions declared such armies dangerous.
papers.m: Hamilton says few state constitutions ban peacetime armies, and the Articles do not. Real dangers exist: British and Spanish territory on the borders, Native nations allied with them, and the need for frontier posts. Militia cannot do this duty for long. The legislature, not the executive, will decide whether to keep an army.
qs: Why does Hamilton think the country will need some troops even in peace?
How does putting army funding in the legislature's hands answer the fear of military rule?
Read Brutus's argument against standing armies (Brutus VIII to X) in summary. Which side do you find stronger, and why?

k.q: standing armies in time of peace
k.w: The phrase at the center of the objection.

k.q: the whole power of raising armies was lodged in the LEGISLATURE, not in the EXECUTIVE
k.w: Congress, not the President, controls the army.

papers.t: The Same Subject Continued (The Powers Necessary to the Common Defense Further Considered)
papers.s: Hamilton argues that defense should not be left to the states, and that banning peacetime armies would only force the government to break its own rules in an emergency.
papers.c: Hamilton continues the military papers.
papers.m: If states provided defense, the burden would fall unequally and states would build armies that could threaten each other and the Union. The militia, though brave, cannot always replace trained troops, as the Revolution showed. A ban on peacetime armies would be ignored when danger came, which would weaken respect for the Constitution itself.
qs: Why would leaving defense to the states be dangerous, in Hamilton's view?
What does Hamilton say about the militia's role in the Revolution?
Why does Hamilton think a rule that cannot be kept is worse than no rule?

k.q: the militia of the country is its natural bulwark
k.w: Hamilton grants the militia's importance.

k.q: War, like most other things, is a science to be acquired and perfected by diligence
k.w: Why trained troops are sometimes needed.

k.q: Wise politicians will be cautious about fettering the government with restrictions that cannot be observed
k.w: His warning about rules that will be broken.

papers.t: The Idea of Restraining the Legislative Authority in Regard to the Common Defense Considered
papers.s: Hamilton argues that the real check on a standing army is that Congress must vote money for it at least every two years.
papers.c: Americans inherited from England a deep suspicion of armies controlled by a king. The English Bill of Rights of 1689 required Parliament's consent for a peacetime army.
papers.m: Hamilton traces the English tradition: the danger was armies controlled by the executive. The Constitution puts the army under the legislature and limits military appropriations to two years. So every two years elected representatives must decide again. Opposition parties and the states will sound the alarm if anything goes wrong.
qs: What is the two-year rule for army appropriations, and why does Hamilton think it matters?
How did English history shape American fears of standing armies?
Is a check that depends on elections enough? What would an Anti-Federalist say?

k.q: The legislature of the United States will be OBLIGED, by this provision, once at least in every two years
k.w: The two-year limit on army funding (Article I, Section 8).

k.q: Schemes to subvert the liberties of a great community REQUIRE TIME to mature them
k.w: Why he thinks a slow plot would be discovered.

papers.t: The Same Subject Continued (The Idea of Restraining the Legislative Authority in Regard to the Common Defense Considered)
papers.s: Hamilton argues that a national government acting directly on citizens will win their respect over time and will rarely need force.
papers.c: Opponents said the national government would need an army to enforce its laws. Hamilton answers that good administration, not force, wins obedience.
papers.m: People obey a government that governs well. The more the national government is part of everyday life, the more familiar and trusted it becomes. Because federal laws will be the supreme law of the land, state officers, including judges, will be bound to help enforce them.
qs: Why does Hamilton think people will come to trust the national government?
How does the Supremacy Clause make state officers part of enforcing federal law?
Is it a good thing or a risk for a distant government to become part of everyday life? Give both sides.

k.q: the more the operations of the national authority are intermingled in the ordinary exercise of government
k.w: Familiarity breeds attachment, he argues.

k.q: the supreme law of the land
k.w: He points to the Supremacy Clause (Article VI).

papers.t: The Same Subject Continued (The Idea of Restraining the Legislative Authority in Regard to the Common Defense Considered)
papers.s: Hamilton argues that force may sometimes be needed, but in a large federal republic the people, the states and the national government can check each other.
papers.c: Hamilton finishes the papers on restraining the legislature in defense matters.
papers.m: Every government may face rebellion. If national rulers betrayed the people, the states would be ready to resist, and the people could shift their support to whichever government protected them. A large country makes it harder for usurpers to crush resistance everywhere at once.
qs: What does Hamilton mean by "power being almost always the rival of power"?
How would the states protect the people against a national government that went wrong?
Compare Madison's similar argument in No. 46.

k.q: If the representatives of the people betray their constituents, there is then no resource left but in the exertion of that original right of self-defense
k.w: Hamilton accepts a right of resistance as a last resort.

k.q: the people, without exaggeration, may be said to be entirely the masters of their own fate
k.w: The states and nation check each other, he says.

k.q: Power being almost always the rival of power
k.w: A short statement of federalism as a check.

papers.t: Concerning the Militia
papers.s: Hamilton defends Congress's power to organize, arm and discipline the militia, while the states appoint its officers and train it.
papers.c: The Constitution (Article I, Section 8) lets Congress provide for organizing, arming and disciplining the militia and calling it out, with the states appointing officers and doing the training. Anti-Federalists feared Congress would neglect the militia or march it far from home. In the newspapers this essay first appeared after Nos. 30 to 36; the 1788 book edition gave it the number used today.
papers.m: Uniform rules make the militia more useful in national defense. Hamilton says it is not practical to train the whole population to a high standard, so a well-trained select corps may be formed, but the people at large will still be armed. Because the states choose the officers, the militia will stay tied to its communities. He dismisses fears of the militia being used against liberty as exaggerated.
qs: How does the Constitution divide power over the militia between Congress and the states?
Why does Hamilton think a "select corps" is a good idea? Why might others have worried about it?
How did the Second Amendment respond to fears about the militia? Read Henry's June 5 speech for one view.

k.q: reserving to the States respectively the appointment of the officers
k.w: The states' share of militia power.

k.q: a well-regulated militia
k.w: A phrase that also appears in the Second Amendment, written the next year.

k.q: the formation of a select corps of moderate extent
k.w: His proposal for a trained part of the militia.

papers.t: Concerning the General Power of Taxation
papers.s: Hamilton begins the taxation papers: money is the lifeblood of government, so Congress needs a general power to tax rather than requisitions from the states.
papers.c: Nos. 30 to 36 deal with the taxing power, one of the most argued-over parts of the Constitution. Anti-Federalists feared that a national power to lay internal taxes would starve the states.
papers.m: A government without its own revenue must either fail in its duties or plunder its people. Requisitions on the states have failed. Limiting Congress to import duties would not be enough in wartime. With a general power to tax, the government can also borrow, because lenders will trust it.
qs: What happened to the Confederation's requisitions on the states?
Why does Hamilton think a government that can tax can also borrow more easily?
Why did some Anti-Federalists want Congress limited to import duties?

k.q: Money is, with propriety, considered as the vital principle of the body politic
k.w: The opening claim of the taxation papers.

k.q: the fallacious and delusive system of quotas and requisitions
k.w: The Articles' method, which Hamilton calls a failure.

papers.t: The Same Subject Continued (Concerning the General Power of Taxation)
papers.s: Hamilton argues from first principles that a government responsible for an unlimited task needs an unlimited power to raise money, and that the states will keep their own taxing power.
papers.c: Hamilton opens with a short essay on reasoning itself.
papers.m: Some truths are as clear as axioms: a government must have the means to do what it is charged with, and the needs of national defense have no fixed limit. Fears that the national government will crush the states are guesses about the future. The states will have the people's attachment, and the people can keep the balance.
qs: What "first principles" does Hamilton start from?
Why does he think fears about the future are not a good reason to deny a power now?
Is it fair to compare political reasoning with geometry? Why or why not?

k.q: In disquisitions of every kind, there are certain primary truths, or first principles
k.w: A rare passage about how to reason about politics.

k.q: as they will hold the scales in their own hands
k.w: He trusts the people to keep the two levels of government in balance.

papers.t: The Same Subject Continued (Concerning the General Power of Taxation)
papers.s: Hamilton explains that the states keep their power to tax, except on imports and exports, because the Constitution gives the nation exclusive power only in three kinds of cases.
papers.c: In the newspapers, this essay and No. 33 appeared as a single paper on January 2, 1788. Supreme Court opinions have often cited this paper on concurrent powers.
papers.m: Hamilton sets out a rule for reading the Constitution: the states keep every power they had unless the Constitution gives it exclusively to the Union. That happens only when the Constitution says so, when it forbids the states, or when a state power would contradict a federal one. Taxation is shared, except for duties on imports and exports.
qs: What are Hamilton's three cases in which a power belongs only to the Union?
What is a "concurrent" power? Give an example.
Why would this paper be useful to judges deciding cases between states and the nation?

k.q: This exclusive delegation, or rather this alienation, of State sovereignty
k.w: The three cases in which states lose a power.

k.q: the State governments would clearly retain all the rights of sovereignty which they before had
k.w: His rule for reading the Constitution.

papers.t: The Same Subject Continued (Concerning the General Power of Taxation)
papers.s: Hamilton defends the Necessary and Proper Clause and the Supremacy Clause, saying they add nothing beyond what any grant of power implies.
papers.c: Anti-Federalists called the Necessary and Proper Clause the "sweeping clause," fearing it could justify any law. The Supremacy Clause makes the Constitution and federal laws the supreme law of the land.
papers.m: Hamilton says a power to make laws must include the power to pass laws needed to carry it out, so the clause only states the obvious. A law is by definition supreme within its scope, but only laws made under the Constitution are supreme. A federal law beyond the government's powers would be "merely acts of usurpation." The people, he adds, are the final judges of whether powers are abused.
qs: Why did Anti-Federalists call the Necessary and Proper Clause the "sweeping clause"?
How does Hamilton limit the reach of the Supremacy Clause?
In McCulloch v. Maryland (1819) the Supreme Court read "necessary" broadly. How does that compare with Hamilton's argument here?

k.q: What is a power, but the ability or faculty of doing a thing?
k.w: His reasoning about implied powers.

k.q: A LAW, by the very meaning of the term, includes supremacy
k.w: Why federal laws must override conflicting state laws.

k.q: merely acts of usurpation
k.w: Laws outside the Constitution have no authority.

papers.t: The Same Subject Continued (Concerning the General Power of Taxation)
papers.s: Hamilton argues that shared taxing power will work, and that the nation must plan for the expenses of future wars, not just present needs.
papers.c: Hamilton points to Rome, where different assemblies with overlapping powers coexisted.
papers.m: Two levels of government can both tax without ruin; the Roman republic had two legislatures that shared power. Hamilton says the states' needs are small compared with the nation's, which must pay for war, the largest expense of any government. Since no one can foresee future dangers, the power should not be limited now.
qs: Why does Hamilton think war is the main reason for national spending?
Is the Roman example a good comparison? Why?
Should a constitution limit a power because it might be abused, or grant it because it might be needed? Make the case for each.

k.q: comitia centuriata
k.w: His Roman example of overlapping assemblies.

k.q: we must bear in mind that we are not to confine our view to the present period, but to look forward to remote futurity
k.w: The paper's main idea.

papers.t: The Same Subject Continued (Concerning the General Power of Taxation)
papers.s: Hamilton argues against limiting federal taxes to certain kinds, and answers the claim that the House will be too small to represent every class of people.
papers.c: Anti-Federalists said a small House would be filled by the wealthy and well-known, not ordinary farmers and tradesmen.
papers.m: Confining the nation to some taxes would load those taxes too heavily. On representation, Hamilton argues that it is "altogether visionary" to have every class represented by its own members. Mechanics and manufacturers trust merchants to speak for them, landholders share common interests, and the learned professions will be neutral. A representative needs to understand his constituents' interests, not share their trade.
qs: Why does Hamilton think representatives do not need to come from every class?
How would Melancton Smith (the Plebeian) or the Federal Farmer answer him?
Is it important that representatives resemble the people they represent? Give arguments on both sides.

k.q: Mechanics and manufacturers will always be inclined, with few exceptions, to give their votes to merchants
k.w: His argument about who will represent whom.

k.q: actual representation of all classes of the people, by persons of each class, is altogether visionary
k.w: The heart of his reply to the Anti-Federalists.

k.q: the learned professions
k.w: He thinks lawyers and others will act as neutral judges between interests.

papers.t: The Same Subject Continued (Concerning the General Power of Taxation)
papers.s: Hamilton finishes the taxation papers: representatives will know enough to tax wisely, double taxation can be avoided, and poll taxes are a resource he hopes never to use.
papers.c: The source edition includes two versions of the closing paragraph, from different editions; both are shown.
papers.m: Hamilton says landholders, merchants and the learned will make up most of the legislature, and they will know the country well enough to tax it. The national government can use state officers and state systems for internal taxes, or leave them to the states when it can. The danger of double taxation is not a good reason to deny the power.
qs: Why does Hamilton think the national government can tax without crushing the states?
What is a poll tax? Why does Hamilton say he does not approve of it but keeps the power anyway?
Why might two versions of the ending appear in different editions?

k.q: I have now gone through the examination of
k.w: The two versions of the closing paragraph begin with these words.

k.q: Happy will it be for ourselves
k.w: The ending of the second version.

papers.t: Concerning the Difficulties of the Convention in Devising a Proper Form of Government
papers.s: Madison explains why the Convention's task was so hard: it had to join energy with liberty, draw lines between powers that cannot be drawn exactly, and balance large and small states.
papers.c: This begins the papers in which Madison examines the plan itself. He writes with unusual humility about the limits of human language and judgment.
papers.m: The Convention had to combine stability and energy with republican liberty. It had to mark the borders between state and national power, and among the branches, though such borders are blurry and words are imperfect. It had to satisfy large and small states. That it reached agreement at all, Madison says, is remarkable.
qs: What were the main difficulties the Convention faced, according to Madison?
Why does Madison say that even the clearest words will leave meaning "more or less obscure"? How does this matter for courts?
Why does Madison ask readers to approach the plan with moderation?

k.q: Among the difficulties encountered by the convention, a very important one must have lain in combining the requisite stability and energy in government
k.w: The central problem the Convention faced.

k.q: no language is so copious as to supply words and phrases for every complex idea
k.w: Madison on the limits of words.

k.q: The real wonder is that so many difficulties should have been surmounted
k.w: He marvels at the agreement reached.

papers.t: The Same Subject Continued, and the Incoherence of the Objections to the New Plan Exposed
papers.s: Madison argues that the Constitution's critics disagree with each other, and that its flaws are small compared with the Articles' defects.
papers.c: Madison notes that ancient lawgivers often founded governments alone, while America chose a convention of many.
papers.m: Madison lists the objections and shows how they contradict each other: some want more power for the House, others less; some want a council for the President, others none. Meanwhile the Articles, which the critics would keep, are far worse. He notes that Congress, under the Articles, was already governing the western territory without clear authority.
qs: What point does Madison make about the critics' disagreements? Is it a fair argument?
Why does he bring up the government of the Western territory?
Could the Anti-Federalists answer that disagreement about remedies does not prove there is no problem?

k.q: It is not a little remarkable that in every case reported by ancient history
k.w: His history of how governments were founded.

k.q: It is not necessary that the former should be perfect; it is sufficient that the latter is more imperfect
k.w: He asks whether perfection is a fair standard for the new plan.

k.q: the Western territory
k.w: Congress's unchecked power there, he says, shows the Articles' weakness.

papers.t: The Conformity of the Plan to Republican Principles
papers.s: Madison argues that the plan is republican, and that it is partly national and partly federal, depending on which part you examine.
papers.c: Critics charged that the Constitution was a national, consolidated government rather than a federal union of states. This paper is Madison's careful answer, and courts and scholars still read it.
papers.m: A republic is a government whose powers come from the people and whose officers serve for limited terms or during good behavior; the Constitution fits. Madison then tests it five ways. Its ratification is federal (each state decides). The House is national; the Senate is federal. Its laws act on individuals (national), but its powers are limited to listed objects (federal). Amendment is a mix. So the plan is "neither a national nor a federal Constitution, but a composition of both."
qs: What is Madison's definition of a republic? Does the Constitution of 1787 meet it fully? (Think about who could vote.)
List Madison's five tests and whether each part is national or federal.
Patrick Henry asked why the Constitution says "We, the people" instead of "We, the states." How would Madison answer?

k.q: we may define a republic to be, or at least may bestow that name on, a government which derives all its powers directly or indirectly from the great body of the people
k.w: Madison's definition of a republic.

k.q: its jurisdiction extends to certain enumerated objects only
k.w: The limit that makes it federal in extent.

k.q: The proposed Constitution, therefore, is, in strictness, neither a national nor a federal Constitution, but a composition of both
k.w: The famous conclusion.

papers.t: On the Powers of the Convention to Form a Mixed Government Examined and Sustained
papers.s: Madison answers the charge that the Convention went beyond its instructions, arguing that it was told to make the government adequate to the Union's needs, and that the people's approval is what counts.
papers.c: Congress and the states had called the Convention "for the sole and express purpose of revising the Articles of Confederation." Critics said the delegates had instead written a new constitution and changed the ratification rule from all thirteen states to nine.
papers.m: Madison reads the instructions together: the Convention was to make the federal government "adequate to the exigencies of Government, and the preservation of the Union." When two parts of an instruction conflict, the more important end should win. In any case the plan is only a proposal, and the people, through ratifying conventions, will decide. He cites the Declaration of Independence's principle that people may alter their governments.
qs: What did the Convention's instructions say? Did the delegates follow them? Present both sides.
Why does Madison say the question matters less because the plan is only a proposal?
The Columbian Patriot and others called the Convention's work a breach of trust. How strong is that charge?

k.q: The powers of the convention ought, in strictness, to be determined by an inspection of the commissions given to the members
k.w: He starts with the actual instructions.

k.q: they were to frame a NATIONAL GOVERNMENT, adequate to the EXIGENCIES OF GOVERNMENT
k.w: How he reads the Convention's mandate.

k.q: the means should be sacrificed to the end
k.w: His rule for reading instructions that conflict.

papers.t: General View of the Powers Conferred by The Constitution
papers.s: Madison begins a review of the powers given to the national government, starting with war, armies, the navy and taxation, and defends the General Welfare Clause as limited by the list that follows it.
papers.c: Nos. 41 to 44 sort the Constitution's powers into six classes. Madison asks two questions: is any power unnecessary, and is the total too much?
papers.m: Security against foreign danger is a basic purpose of government, and its powers cannot be safely limited, since enemies set the measure of what is needed. The best protection against standing armies is the Union itself. On the taxing clause, Madison argues that the words "to provide for the common defense and general welfare" are explained and limited by the specific powers listed after them, and do not grant unlimited power.
qs: What are the two questions Madison asks about the powers?
How does Madison read the words "general welfare"? Hamilton later read the taxing and spending power more broadly. What is the difference?
Why does Madison say the Union itself is the best defense against standing armies?

k.q: Security against foreign danger is one of the primitive objects of civil society
k.w: The first class of powers.

k.q: How could a readiness for war in time of peace be safely prohibited
k.w: Why a peacetime ban on armies would fail.

k.q: Had no other enumeration or definition of the powers of the Congress been found in the Constitution
k.w: Madison's reading of the General Welfare Clause.

papers.t: The Powers Conferred by the Constitution Further Considered
papers.s: Madison reviews foreign relations and commerce powers, the clause on the slave trade, and powers that keep peace among the states, such as regulating interstate commerce, coinage, naturalization and bankruptcy.
papers.c: Article I, Section 9 barred Congress from prohibiting the importation of enslaved people before 1808. This was one of the compromises made at the Convention with the delegates from South Carolina and Georgia. Federalist 42 is among the papers the Supreme Court has quoted most often.
papers.m: Treaties, ambassadors and the law of nations belong to the Union. Madison says it would have been better to allow an end to the importation of enslaved people at once, but calls the 1808 date a great point gained, since Congress could then end the trade. He answers critics who used the clause against the Constitution from opposite directions. Power over commerce among the states will stop states from taxing each other's trade.
qs: Why did the Convention protect the importation of enslaved people until 1808? How does Madison describe the clause?
What problem was the interstate commerce power meant to solve?
Pick one power from this paper (coinage, naturalization, bankruptcy, post roads) and explain why Madison thinks it belongs to the Union.

k.q: It were doubtless to be wished, that the power of prohibiting the importation of slaves had not been postponed until the year 1808
k.w: Madison on the slave-trade clause. Congress did ban the import trade, effective January 1, 1808; slavery itself continued until the Thirteenth Amendment in 1865.

k.q: The defect of power in the existing Confederacy to regulate the commerce between its several members
k.w: The origin of the Commerce Clause's interstate part.

k.q: The dissimilarity in the rules of naturalization has long been remarked as a fault
k.w: Why naturalization rules should be uniform.

papers.t: The Same Subject Continued (The Powers Conferred by the Constitution Further Considered)
papers.s: Madison reviews a group of other powers: copyrights and patents, the seat of government, treason, new states, the territories, the guarantee of republican government, debts, amendment, and ratification by nine states.
papers.c: This is a long tour of smaller clauses, several of which later mattered a great deal, such as the admission of new states and the amendment process.
papers.m: Madison defends each clause briefly. Copyrights and patents reward authors and inventors. The national government needs control of its own capital. Treason is narrowly defined so it cannot be stretched. The Union must protect each state's republican government against invasion and violence. The amendment process guards equally against making changes too easily and too hard. Ratification by nine states is justified by necessity and by the people's right to replace a failed government.
qs: Why does Madison think the definition of treason needed to be narrow?
What does "guarantee to every State a republican form of government" mean? Why did Madison think it was needed?
How does Madison justify putting the Constitution into effect with nine states instead of all thirteen?

k.q: The copyright of authors has been solemnly adjudged, in Great Britain, to be a right of common law
k.w: The background of the Copyright and Patent Clause.

k.q: guards equally against that extreme facility, which would render the Constitution too mutable
k.w: Madison's balanced view of the amendment process.

k.q: the great principle of self-preservation
k.w: His answer to why nine states may go ahead without the others.

papers.t: Restrictions on the Authority of the Several States
papers.s: Madison explains the limits on the states, such as no coining money or impairing contracts, and defends the Necessary and Proper Clause and the Supremacy Clause.
papers.c: Madison had been troubled by state laws in the 1780s that he thought unjust, such as paper-money and debt-relief laws. The Necessary and Proper Clause was one of the most attacked parts of the plan.
papers.m: Bans on state bills of credit, ex post facto laws, bills of attainder and laws impairing contracts protect property and trust between states. Madison says the Necessary and Proper Clause is unavoidable: no list could name every means, and without the clause the powers would still imply the means. If Congress abuses it, the courts, the executive and above all the people at elections can correct it. Without the Supremacy Clause, the Constitution would be a monster with the head under the direction of the members.
qs: Why does Madison approve of the bans on state paper money and laws impairing contracts?
What are the four other ways the Convention could have handled the Necessary and Proper Clause, and why did Madison reject them?
If Congress misuses this clause, what remedies does Madison name?

k.q: Bills of attainder, ex post facto laws, and laws impairing the obligation of contracts, are contrary to the first principles of the social compact
k.w: Why the Constitution limits state power here.

k.q: No axiom is more clearly established in law, or in reason, than that wherever the end is required, the means are authorized
k.w: His defense of implied powers.

k.q: it would have seen the authority of the whole society every where subordinate to the authority of the parts
k.w: Why the Constitution must be supreme.

papers.t: The Alleged Danger From the Powers of the Union to the State Governments Considered
papers.s: Madison argues that the states have little to fear from the Union: the national government's powers are few and defined, while the states' are numerous and indefinite.
papers.c: This paper contains one of the most quoted descriptions of federalism. Courts still cite it in cases about the balance between state and national power.
papers.m: Madison says the goal of government is the welfare of the people, not the dignity of the states. History shows confederacies breaking apart, not swallowing their members. The states will have more officers, more influence and more of the people's affection, and they help choose the national government. National powers are mostly about war, peace, trade and taxes; everyday matters stay with the states.
qs: What does Madison mean by "few and defined" and "numerous and indefinite"?
Does the national government today fit Madison's description? Give an example for and against.
Why does Madison put the people's welfare above the sovereignty of the states?

k.q: the real welfare of the great body of the people, is the supreme object to be pursued
k.w: Madison's measure for judging any government.

k.q: The powers delegated by the proposed Constitution to the federal government, are few and defined
k.w: The famous sentence on federalism.

k.q: The operations of the federal government will be most extensive and important in times of war and danger
k.w: His prediction about how the balance would work.

papers.t: The Influence of the State and Federal Governments Compared
papers.s: Madison argues that the people's loyalty will favor the states, and that if the national government overreached, the states and an armed population could resist.
papers.c: Madison continues No. 45, comparing the strength of state and national governments.
papers.m: Both governments are agents of the people. The people will favor the one that serves them better, which is likely to be the states. Members of Congress will often bring state loyalties with them. If the national government tried to take power, the states would sound the alarm and coordinate resistance. A regular army could not overcome a militia of half a million armed citizens led by officers chosen by the states.
qs: What does Madison mean when he calls both governments "agents and trustees of the people"?
How would the states resist federal overreach, according to Madison?
Compare this paper with Hamilton's No. 28. What do they agree on?

k.q: The federal and State governments are in fact but different agents and trustees of the people
k.w: Madison's view of where sovereignty rests.

k.q: ambitious encroachments of the federal government, on the authority of the State governments, would not excite the opposition of a single State, or of a few States only
k.w: How the states would resist together.

k.q: the advantage of being armed, which the Americans possess over the people of almost every other nation
k.w: A passage often cited in Second Amendment debates.

papers.t: The Particular Structure of the New Government and the Distribution of Power Among Its Different Parts
papers.s: Madison answers the charge that the Constitution mixes the branches together, explaining what Montesquieu's maxim of separation of powers really requires.
papers.c: Critics said the Senate's share in appointments and treaties, and the President's veto, broke the rule that legislative, executive and judicial powers must be separate. Nos. 47 to 51 are Madison's answer.
papers.m: Madison agrees that putting all three powers in the same hands is "the very definition of tyranny." But Montesquieu, studying Britain, did not mean the branches could have no part in each other's work. He meant that the whole power of one branch should not be held by those who hold the whole power of another. Every state constitution blends the branches somewhat.
qs: What exactly does the separation-of-powers maxim forbid, according to Madison?
Why does Madison review the state constitutions?
Centinel preferred a simple government with one legislature. How does that view differ from Madison's?

k.q: The accumulation of all powers, legislative, executive, and judiciary, in the same hands
k.w: The famous definition of tyranny.

k.q: The oracle who is always consulted and cited on this subject is the celebrated Montesquieu
k.w: Madison takes back Montesquieu from the opponents.

k.q: where the WHOLE power of one department is exercised by the same hands which possess the WHOLE power of another department
k.w: What the maxim really forbids.

papers.t: These Departments Should Not Be So Far Separated as to Have No Constitutional Control Over Each Other
papers.s: Madison argues that written boundaries between the branches are not enough, because the legislature especially tends to draw all power into its "impetuous vortex."
papers.c: Madison draws on the experience of Virginia and Pennsylvania, where legislatures had overstepped their limits.
papers.m: Marking the branches' borders on paper, "parchment barriers," will not stop encroachment. In a republic the legislature is the strongest branch and the most likely to grab power. Madison quotes Jefferson's Notes on the State of Virginia: 173 despots would surely be as oppressive as one. So the branches must be connected enough to check each other.
qs: What are "parchment barriers"? Why does Madison think they are not enough?
Why does Madison see the legislature as the greatest danger in a republic?
Do you agree that the legislature is the most dangerous branch today? Explain.

k.q: parchment barriers
k.w: Why written rules alone fail.

k.q: The legislative department is everywhere extending the sphere of its activity, and drawing all power into its impetuous vortex
k.w: Madison's view of the most dangerous branch.

k.q: An elective despotism was not the government we fought for
k.w: He quotes Jefferson.

papers.t: Method of Guarding Against the Encroachments of Any One Department of Government by Appealing to the People Through a Convention
papers.s: Madison considers Jefferson's idea of calling a convention whenever two branches agree that the Constitution has been broken, and rejects it as unsettling and unlikely to work.
papers.c: This is one of the twelve once-disputed papers; most scholars now credit Madison. Jefferson had proposed the idea in his draft constitution for Virginia.
papers.m: Madison respects the idea, since the people are the source of power. But frequent appeals to the people would suggest the government is flawed and weaken the respect that time gives to any government. They would stir up passions, and the legislature, with its many members close to the people, would usually win.
qs: What was Jefferson's proposal, and why does Madison think it would not work?
What does Madison mean when he says governments need the "veneration which time bestows on every thing"?
Should constitutions be hard or easy to change? Use this paper and No. 43 in your answer.

k.q: As the people are the only legitimate fountain of power
k.w: Madison's starting point.

k.q: every appeal to the people would carry an implication of some defect in the government
k.w: Why frequent appeals are risky.

k.q: it is the reason, alone, of the public, that ought to control and regulate the government
k.w: Reason, not passion, should rule.

papers.t: Periodical Appeals to the People Considered
papers.s: Madison rejects regular, scheduled reviews of the Constitution, using Pennsylvania's Council of Censors as an example of how such reviews get caught up in party politics.
papers.c: Pennsylvania's 1776 constitution created a Council of Censors to meet every seven years and check whether the constitution had been obeyed. It met in 1783–1784. This is one of the once-disputed papers.
papers.m: Reviews at short intervals would be too close to the events; at long intervals, too late to help. Pennsylvania's council was divided by party, and its findings were ignored. So periodic appeals to the people are not a good way to keep the branches in their places.
qs: What was the Council of Censors, and what does Madison say went wrong with it?
Why does Madison think scheduled reviews would fail either way, short or long?
Centinel praised Pennsylvania's constitution. How might he answer Madison?

k.q: the Council of Censors which met in Pennsylvania in 1783 and 1784
k.w: Madison's real-world example.

k.q: the existence of the disease, and by its example, the inefficacy of the remedy
k.w: Madison's verdict on the council.

papers.t: The Structure of the Government Must Furnish the Proper Checks and Balances Between the Different Departments
papers.s: Madison explains how the structure of the government will keep each branch in check: ambition must be made to counteract ambition.
papers.c: This is one of the most read of all the papers. It is one of the twelve once disputed between Hamilton and Madison; most scholars now credit Madison.
papers.m: Since written barriers are not enough, each branch must have the means and the motive to resist the others. "Ambition must be made to counteract ambition." This is needed because people are not angels. The legislature is divided into two houses, the executive gets a qualified veto, and the federal system splits power between nation and states, giving a "double security" to the people's rights. In a large republic, many interests make it hard for a majority to oppress a minority.
qs: Explain "ambition must be made to counteract ambition" in your own words, with an example from the Constitution.
Why does Madison say "if men were angels, no government would be necessary"? What view of human nature does this show?
What is the "double security"?
Compare this paper's argument about a large republic with No. 10.

k.q: Ambition must be made to counteract ambition
k.w: The core idea of checks and balances.

k.q: If men were angels, no government would be necessary
k.w: Perhaps the most quoted sentence in the series.

k.q: you must first enable the government to control the governed; and in the next place oblige it to control itself
k.w: The double task of a constitution.

k.q: a double security arises to the rights of the people
k.w: Federalism as a second layer of protection.

k.q: Justice is the end of government
k.w: The purpose behind the machinery.

papers.t: The House of Representatives
papers.s: The paper begins the study of the House of Representatives: who may vote and serve, and why two-year terms keep members dependent on the people.
papers.c: Nos. 52 to 61 cover the House. Many states then elected their assemblies every year, and Anti-Federalists favored annual elections. This is one of the once-disputed papers; most scholars now credit Madison.
papers.m: Voters for the House are the same people who vote for the largest branch of their state legislature, so the states' own rules decide. Members must be at least 25, citizens for seven years, and residents of their state. The House must have "an immediate dependence on, and an intimate sympathy with, the people," and frequent elections secure that. History, from Britain to the colonies, shows that two years is safe.
qs: Who decided who could vote for the House under the original Constitution? How has that changed since, through amendments?
Why does Madison think two-year terms are frequent enough?
Many Anti-Federalists preferred one-year terms. Make the best case for annual elections.

k.q: The qualifications of the elected, being less carefully and properly defined by the State constitutions
k.w: The qualifications for House members.

k.q: an immediate dependence on, and an intimate sympathy with, the people
k.w: The purpose of frequent elections.

k.q: Let us bring our inquiries nearer home
k.w: He turns to the colonies' experience.

papers.t: The Same Subject Continued (The House of Representatives)
papers.s: The paper answers the saying "where annual elections end, tyranny begins," arguing that national lawmakers need two years to learn their work.
papers.c: This is one of the once-disputed papers, now generally credited to Madison.
papers.m: The saying made sense in Britain, where Parliament could extend its own term. In America the Constitution fixes terms, and Congress cannot change them. A federal lawmaker must learn about laws, trade and conditions in all thirteen states, and foreign affairs too; one year is not enough. Two-year terms also limit the harm of contested elections that take time to settle.
qs: Why did the saying about annual elections make sense in Britain, according to the paper?
What does a national legislator need to know that a state legislator might not?
Do longer terms make lawmakers wiser or less accountable? Argue both sides.

k.q: where annual elections end, tyranny begins
k.w: The saying Madison answers.

k.q: a Constitution established by the people and unalterable by the government
k.w: The key difference from Britain.

k.q: No man can be a competent legislator who does not add to an upright intention and a sound judgment a certain degree of knowledge
k.w: Why experience matters.

papers.t: The Apportionment of Members Among the States
papers.s: The paper explains the three-fifths clause, which counted three of every five enslaved people for both representation and direct taxes, by presenting the argument a Southern advocate would make.
papers.c: Article I, Section 2 counted "three fifths of all other Persons" (enslaved people) when apportioning House seats and direct taxes among the states. It was a compromise between delegates who wanted enslaved people counted fully for representation and those who wanted them not counted at all. The clause was replaced by the Fourteenth Amendment in 1868. This is one of the once-disputed papers; most scholars now credit Madison.
papers.m: The author voices the argument of "one of our Southern brethren": the law treats enslaved people partly as persons and partly as property, so the Constitution's compromise counts them partly. Since the same rule applies to taxes, the author says it is balanced. He admits the reasoning "may appear to be a little strained in some points," but says it reconciles him to the rule. Readers then and now have judged this reasoning very differently.
qs: What did the three-fifths clause count, and what two things did it affect?
Why does the author present this argument in the voice of a Southern advocate? What does that choice suggest?
Look at Mason's Objections and his complaint about the slave trade. How did slavery divide even those who agreed on other questions?
Which later amendment replaced this clause, and when?

k.q: the mixed character of persons and of property
k.w: The heart of the argument presented.

k.q: Such is the reasoning which an advocate for the Southern interests might employ on this subject
k.w: Notice that the author frames the argument as someone else's.

k.q: In one respect, the establishment of a common measure for representation and taxation will have a very salutary effect
k.w: Why tying representation to taxes was meant to keep states honest in their counts.

papers.t: The Total Number of the House of Representatives
