papers.s: The paper answers the charge that a House of 65 members is too small to be safe, arguing that very large assemblies become mobs and that the House will grow with the population.
papers.c: The first House was to have 65 members, about one for every 30,000 people at most. Anti-Federalists said so few could be bribed or would ignore ordinary people. Mosteller and Wallace found the statistical evidence weakest for this paper, though it still pointed to Madison.
papers.m: There is no exact right size. Too few members can be corrupted; too many become a crowd. "Had every Athenian citizen been a Socrates, every Athenian assembly would still have been a mob." Sixty-five is a start, and the number will rise with each census. The House cannot easily be bribed by foreign powers, the Senate or the President.
qs: Why does the author think a very large assembly would be a problem?
How does this paper's view of human nature compare with No. 51's "if men were angels"?
The House has had 435 members since 1913 (except briefly). Is that too many or too few for today's population? Use the paper's reasoning.

k.q: Had every Athenian citizen been a Socrates, every Athenian assembly would still have been a mob
k.w: Why size alone does not make an assembly wise.

k.q: As there is a degree of depravity in mankind which requires a certain degree of circumspection and distrust
k.w: A balanced view of human nature.

k.q: Republican government presupposes the existence of these qualities in a higher degree than any other form
k.w: Self-government depends on trust and virtue.

papers.t: The Same Subject Continued (The Total Number of the House of Representatives)
papers.s: The paper argues that a small House can still know enough about the people's interests, because federal laws deal mainly with trade, taxes and the militia.
papers.c: This is one of the once-disputed papers. The source edition shows two versions of two paragraphs, from different editions.
papers.m: A representative should understand his constituents' circumstances, but only those that federal law touches. Commerce, taxes and the militia need general knowledge, not knowledge of every county. Members will bring knowledge of their state laws with them. Britain's House of Commons, with many fewer members per person, has protected liberty.
qs: What kinds of knowledge does the author think a federal representative needs?
Why might the Federal Farmer disagree that a few representatives could know enough?
Why do some editions show two versions of these paragraphs?

k.q: It is a sound and important principle that the representative ought to be acquainted with the interests and circumstances of his constituents
k.w: The principle both sides accepted.

k.q: The experience of Great Britain
k.w: His comparison.

papers.t: The Alleged Tendency of the New Plan to Elevate the Few at the Expense of the Many Considered in Connection with Representation
papers.s: The paper answers the charge that the House will be run by a wealthy few: the electors are the many, anyone may be chosen, and members must live under the laws they make.
papers.c: Anti-Federalists, including the Federal Farmer and Melancton Smith, argued that large districts would favor the rich and famous. This is one of the once-disputed papers.
papers.m: The electors are "not the rich, more than the poor," and any citizen of merit can be chosen. Representatives will be bound by gratitude, ambition for re-election, and frequent elections. Above all, they "can make no law which will not have its full operation on themselves and their friends." State senates and governors are chosen by large districts, too, without becoming aristocracies.
qs: What five reasons does the author give for trusting representatives?
Why did Anti-Federalists think large districts would favor the wealthy? Is that a reasonable fear?
Does Congress today usually live under the laws it passes? Find an example.

k.q: The aim of every political constitution is, or ought to be, first to obtain for rulers men who possess most wisdom to discern, and most virtue to pursue, the common good
k.w: The double aim of a constitution.

k.q: Not the rich, more than the poor; not the learned, more than the ignorant
k.w: Who the electors are.

k.q: they can make no law which will not have its full operation on themselves and their friends
k.w: A key safeguard.

papers.t: Objection That The Number of Members Will Not Be Augmented as the Progress of Population Demands Considered
papers.s: The paper answers the fear that the House will not grow as the population grows, pointing to the census and to the House's power over money; it also defends majority rule.
papers.c: This is one of the once-disputed papers. The Constitution requires a census every ten years to reapportion House seats.
papers.m: The census will force a new count every ten years. Large states will push for more seats, and the House holds "the power of the purse," the strongest tool in any constitution. The paper also argues against requiring more than a majority for laws, since that would let a minority rule.
qs: Why is the power over money so important?
How does the census protect the growth of representation?
When might requiring a supermajority be wise? When might it let a minority rule?

k.q: Within every successive term of ten years a census of inhabitants is to be repeated
k.w: The census as a safeguard.

k.q: This power over the purse may, in fact, be regarded as the most complete and effectual weapon
k.w: The House's control of money.

k.q: the fundamental principle of free government would be reversed
k.w: Why the author opposes supermajority rules.

papers.t: Concerning the Power of Congress to Regulate the Election of Members
papers.s: Hamilton defends Congress's power to alter state rules on the times, places and manner of federal elections, saying every government must be able to preserve itself.
papers.c: Article I, Section 4 lets state legislatures set the times, places and manner of congressional elections, but Congress may make or alter those rules. Anti-Federalists warned that Congress could move polling places to rig elections.
papers.m: Hamilton says the power had to rest somewhere, and leaving it only to the states would let them destroy the national government by refusing to hold elections. "Every government ought to contain in itself the means of its own preservation." Congress's power is a backstop.
qs: What does the Elections Clause allow the states and Congress to do?
Why does Hamilton think leaving the power only to the states would be dangerous?
Cato VII and Centinel feared Congress would use this power to control elections. Which fear seems more reasonable to you, and why?

k.q: every government ought to contain in itself the means of its own preservation
k.w: The principle behind the clause.

k.q: Nothing can be more evident, than that an exclusive power of regulating elections for the national government, in the hands of the State legislatures, would leave the existence of the Union entirely at their mercy
k.w: The danger he wants to avoid.

papers.t: The Same Subject Continued (Concerning the Power of Congress to Regulate the Election of Members)
papers.s: Hamilton argues that Congress could not use its election power to favor the rich or any class, because the people, the states and the Senate's structure stand in the way.
papers.c: Hamilton continues the defense of the Elections Clause.
papers.m: The clause covers only times, places and manner, not who may vote or serve. The House, Senate and President are chosen in different ways by different bodies, so no single faction could control them all. Any attempt to rig elections would provoke the people and the states.
qs: What is the difference between regulating the "manner" of elections and deciding who may vote?
Why does Hamilton think different ways of choosing each branch protect against capture?
What would an Anti-Federalist say about trusting Congress not to abuse this power?

k.q: an uncontrollable power over the elections to the federal government could not, without hazard, be committed to the State legislatures
k.w: His starting point.

k.q: The improbability of the attempt may be satisfactorily inferred from this single reflection
k.w: Why he thinks abuse is unlikely.

papers.t: The Same Subject Continued (Concerning the Power of Congress to Regulate the Election of Members)
papers.s: Hamilton finishes the Elections Clause papers, comparing it with state constitutions and arguing for a uniform national election day.
papers.c: New York's own constitution let the legislature regulate elections. Hamilton points this out.
papers.m: Several state constitutions give their legislatures similar powers without harm. A uniform time for elections would help elect a House whose members change together, which keeps out factional spirit.
qs: How does Hamilton use New York's own constitution against the objection?
Congress later set one day for federal elections. Why might a uniform day matter?

k.q: THE more candid opposers of the provision respecting elections
k.w: He begins by granting his opponents some credit.

k.q: Uniformity in the time of elections seems not less requisite
k.w: The case for one election day.

papers.t: The Senate
papers.s: The paper explains the Senate: older members with longer citizenship, chosen by state legislatures, with equal votes for each state, to bring stability and wisdom to lawmaking.
papers.c: Under the original Constitution, state legislatures chose senators. The Seventeenth Amendment (1913) moved that choice to the voters. This is one of the once-disputed papers; most scholars now credit Madison.
papers.m: Senators must be 30 and citizens for nine years. Choice by state legislatures gives the states a role. Equal votes for each state were a compromise and a recognition of the states' remaining sovereignty. A second chamber guards against hasty, passion-driven laws and against "mutable" policy that changes too often. Unstable laws hurt the honest and help the clever.
qs: Why does each state have two senators regardless of size? Present the reasons given at the time and a modern criticism.
What does the paper mean by "mutable" government? Why is it harmful?
The Seventeenth Amendment changed how senators are chosen. What reasons were given for it?

k.q: the equal vote allowed to each State is at once a constitutional recognition of the portion of sovereignty remaining in the individual States
k.w: Why each state gets two senators.

k.q: A good government implies two things
k.w: Fidelity to the people's happiness, and knowledge of how to pursue it.

k.q: It will be of little avail to the people, that the laws are made by men of their own choice, if the laws be so voluminous that they cannot be read
k.w: A famous warning against unstable, complicated laws.

papers.t: The Senate Continued
papers.s: The paper argues that a Senate with long terms helps the nation keep its reputation abroad, take long-term responsibility, and resist temporary popular errors.
papers.c: This is one of the once-disputed papers. The author looks at ancient republics, nearly all of which had a senate.
papers.m: A small, stable body can care about national character and be held responsible for long-term policy. There are moments when the people, misled, demand measures they will later regret; then "the cool and deliberate sense of the community" needs a body that can slow things down. The Senate is not a threat to liberty: it is elected, and the House and the people can check it.
qs: Why does the author think the people sometimes need protection from their own passing mistakes? Is this a democratic or undemocratic idea? Explain both views.
What does he mean by "the total exclusion of the people, in their collective capacity"?
How does the author answer the fear that the Senate will become an aristocracy?

k.q: the cool and deliberate sense of the community
k.w: What the Senate is meant to protect.

k.q: the total exclusion of the people, in their collective capacity
k.w: What the author says makes American government different from the ancient republics.

k.q: liberty may be endangered by the abuses of liberty as well as by the abuses of power
k.w: A two-sided warning.

papers.t: The Powers of the Senate
papers.s: Jay defends giving the President and the Senate together the power to make treaties, with two-thirds of senators agreeing.
papers.c: This was Jay's last paper; illness had kept him from writing more. He was an expert in foreign affairs and had negotiated the 1783 peace treaty.
papers.m: Treaties need knowledgeable, stable negotiators, and sometimes secrecy and speed. Senators chosen by legislatures, serving long terms, and a President chosen by electors are likely to be capable. Treaties are binding like laws, but they cannot be changed by one side alone, because they are agreements with other nations. The two-thirds rule guards against corruption.
qs: Why did the Constitution leave the House out of treaty-making?
Why does Jay think treaties should be binding as law?
Mason objected that treaties could become supreme law without the House. How might Jay answer?

k.q: perfect SECRECY and immediate DESPATCH
k.w: Why the House is not part of treaty-making.

k.q: they who make treaties may alter or cancel them; but still let us not forget that treaties are made, not by only one of the contracting parties, but by both
k.w: Why treaties differ from ordinary laws.

papers.t: The Powers of the Senate Continued
papers.s: Hamilton explains why the Senate tries impeachments: such cases are political, and the Senate is the body most likely to be fair and independent.
papers.c: The House impeaches (charges) and the Senate tries officials, with a two-thirds vote needed to convict. This paper is often quoted during impeachments.
papers.m: Impeachable offenses come from "the abuse or violation of some public trust" and are political in nature, so the trial will stir up parties. The tribunal must be dignified and independent. The Supreme Court is too small and might later judge the same person in a criminal trial. The Senate fits best, though no choice is perfect.
qs: What kinds of offenses does Hamilton think impeachment is for?
Why does he think the Supreme Court should not try impeachments?
Hamilton warns that impeachment will divide the country into parties. Why?

k.q: those offenses which proceed from the misconduct of public men, or, in other words, from the abuse or violation of some public trust
k.w: Hamilton's description of impeachable offenses.

k.q: They are of a nature which may with peculiar propriety be denominated POLITICAL
k.w: Why impeachment is political.

k.q: Where else than in the Senate could have been found a tribunal sufficiently dignified, or sufficiently independent?
k.w: His case for the Senate.

papers.t: Objections to the Power of the Senate To Set as a Court for Impeachments Further Considered
papers.s: Hamilton answers objections to the Senate's role in impeachments: that it mixes powers, makes the Senate too strong, and puts senators in judgment of officials they helped appoint.
papers.c: Hamilton continues No. 65.
papers.m: Some mixing of powers is needed for checks to work. The House's sole power to impeach and its control of money balance the Senate. Senators who approved an appointment will not be biased in favor of an official who later misbehaves, since the President chose him. Senators trying treaties they helped make will still be judged by public opinion.
qs: List the objections Hamilton answers. Which answer is strongest?
Why might senators be poor judges of officials they voted to confirm? How does Hamilton respond?

k.q: a partial intermixture of those departments for special purposes
k.w: Hamilton's answer to the mixing objection.

k.q: the most popular branch
k.w: He describes the House's strength.

papers.t: The Executive Department
papers.s: Hamilton begins the papers on the presidency by accusing critics of painting the President as a king, and corrects one claim about filling Senate vacancies.
papers.c: Nos. 67 to 77 cover the executive. Many Americans feared any strong single executive after their experience with royal governors and King George III.
papers.m: Hamilton says opponents have exaggerated the President's powers, comparing him to a monarch with crowns and courtiers. He picks one example: a claim that the President could fill vacancies in the Senate. He shows that the clause on recess appointments covers only offices whose appointments are "not herein otherwise provided for," and senators are chosen by state legislatures.
qs: What was the claim about filling Senate vacancies, and how does Hamilton answer it?
Why were Americans in 1787 so worried about a single executive?
Read Cato IV or Henry's June 5 speech. Is the comparison of the President to a king fair or exaggerated? Give both views.

k.q: the writers against the Constitution seem to have taken pains to signalize their talent of misrepresentation
k.w: Hamilton's charge against the critics.

k.q: The second clause of the second section of the second article empowers the President
k.w: The clause at issue: recess appointments.

papers.t: The Mode of Electing the President
papers.s: Hamilton defends the Electoral College: electors chosen for one purpose will weigh the candidates with care, and the process will favor able and well-known men.
papers.c: Under the original plan, each state chose electors in the manner its legislature directed; the electors voted for two people, and the runner-up became Vice President. The Twelfth Amendment (1804) changed this to separate votes for President and Vice President.
papers.m: Hamilton says the people's sense should count, but the final choice should be made by men chosen for that task, meeting in their own states to avoid intrigue and foreign meddling. Because electors meet once and then disband, they are hard to corrupt. The process will rarely elevate someone with only "talents for low intrigue, and the little arts of popularity." He notes that opponents attacked this part of the plan less than any other.
qs: What problems was the Electoral College designed to avoid, according to Hamilton?
How did the Twelfth Amendment change the process?
People today disagree about the Electoral College. List the main arguments for keeping it and for replacing it with a national popular vote, without choosing a side.

k.q: THE mode of appointment of the Chief Magistrate of the United States is almost the only part of the system
k.w: Hamilton's opening claim that this part drew little criticism.

k.q: if the manner of it be not perfect, it is at least excellent
k.w: His confident judgment, with a word that differs between editions.

k.q: Talents for low intrigue, and the little arts of popularity
k.w: What the electors are meant to screen out.

papers.t: The Real Character of the Executive
papers.s: Hamilton compares the President with the king of Great Britain and the governor of New York to show that the President's powers are limited.
papers.c: Hamilton aims this at New York readers, who knew their own governor's powers well.
papers.m: Hamilton goes power by power. The President is elected for four years, the king rules for life by inheritance. The President can be impeached; the king is "sacred and inviolable." The President's veto can be overridden; the king's is absolute. The President commands the military but cannot declare war or raise armies; the king can do both. The President makes treaties and appointments only with the Senate. In several points, Hamilton argues, the President has less power than the governor of New York.
qs: Make a chart of Hamilton's comparisons between the President and the king.
How does Hamilton describe the commander-in-chief power? How have scholars and Presidents since disagreed about its reach?
Why does Hamilton compare the President with New York's governor?

k.q: The President of the United States would be liable to be impeached, tried, and, upon conviction
k.w: Accountability the king did not have.

k.q: nothing more than the supreme command and direction of the military and naval forces
k.w: How Hamilton describes the commander-in-chief power.

k.q: The President of the United States would be an officer elected by the people for FOUR years
k.w: The paper's closing summary of differences.

papers.t: The Executive Department Further Considered
papers.s: Hamilton's famous defense of a single, energetic executive: one person acts with decision and speed, and cannot hide behind a council.
papers.c: Some Anti-Federalists, and some delegates at the Convention, wanted a plural executive or an executive council. This paper is among the most cited by courts and scholars on presidential power.
papers.m: "Energy in the Executive is a leading character in the definition of good government." Energy needs unity, duration, adequate pay and competent powers; safety needs dependence on the people and responsibility. One person brings "decision, activity, secrecy, and despatch." A plural executive or a council splits responsibility, so the public cannot tell whom to blame. Unity makes the executive accountable as well as strong.
qs: What four things make up "energy" in the executive, and what two make up "safety"?
Why does Hamilton oppose an executive council? Mason wanted one. Compare their reasons.
Courts and scholars still argue about how much power the President should have. How might a supporter of strong executive power use this paper? How might a critic answer?

k.q: Energy in the Executive is a leading character in the definition of good government
k.w: The opening thesis.

k.q: A feeble Executive implies a feeble execution of the government
k.w: The danger of a weak executive.

k.q: Decision, activity, secrecy, and despatch will generally characterize the proceedings of one man
k.w: Why one is better than many in the executive.

k.q: Responsibility is of two kinds
k.w: Unity makes it easier to blame or punish.

papers.t: The Duration in Office of the Executive
papers.s: Hamilton argues that a four-year term gives the President enough independence to resist passing public moods and legislative pressure.
papers.c: Duration is the second ingredient of executive energy Hamilton named in No. 70.
papers.m: A short term would make the President timid. The people "commonly intend the public good," but they can be misled, and the President should be able to resist momentary impulses until reflection returns. He must also resist the legislature. Four years is long enough to give some firmness, but not so long as to threaten liberty.
qs: Why does Hamilton think the President should sometimes resist public opinion?
Is four years too long, too short, or about right? Use the paper's reasons.
How does this paper's view of the people compare with No. 63's?

k.q: The republican principle demands that the deliberate sense of the community should govern
k.w: The deliberate sense, not momentary impulse.

k.q: the people commonly INTEND the PUBLIC GOOD
k.w: Hamilton's trust and caution about the people.

k.q: It cannot be affirmed, that a duration of four years, or any other limited duration, would completely answer the end proposed
k.w: He admits no term is perfect.

papers.t: The Same Subject Continued, and Re-Eligibility of the Executive Considered
papers.s: Hamilton argues against term limits for the President: re-eligibility rewards good conduct, keeps experience, and avoids dangerous temptations.
papers.c: The original Constitution set no limit on presidential terms. Washington chose to serve two, and the Twenty-second Amendment (1951) set a two-term limit.
papers.m: Hamilton lists five harms of barring re-election: less reason to behave well, temptation to grab what one can before leaving, loss of experienced leaders in a crisis, needless changes in policy, and pushing out men the people want to keep. The benefits claimed, more independence and safety, are doubtful. It is an "excess of refinement" to deny the people a choice they want.
qs: List Hamilton's five harms of term limits. Which is strongest?
The Twenty-second Amendment adopted a two-term limit. What reasons were given for it?
Make the best case for and against term limits for members of Congress, which some people support today.

k.q: Nothing appears more plausible at first sight, nor more ill-founded upon close inspection
k.w: His view of term limits.

k.q: One ill effect of the exclusion would be a diminution of the inducements to good behavior
k.w: The first of five harms.

k.q: There is an excess of refinement in the idea of disabling the people to continue in office men who had entitled themselves
k.w: The closing argument.

papers.t: The Provision For The Support of the Executive, and the Veto Power
papers.s: Hamilton defends a fixed presidential salary and the qualified veto, which guards against hasty or unwise laws and protects the executive from the legislature.
papers.c: The President's pay cannot be raised or cut during the term. The veto can be overridden by two-thirds of each house. New York had a similar veto, held by a Council of Revision.
papers.m: A fixed salary keeps the legislature from bending the President by controlling his pay, since "a power over a man's support is a power over his will." The veto lets the President defend his office against legislative intrusion and adds a check against bad laws passed in haste or by faction. Because it can be overridden, the President will be more willing to use it than a king with an absolute veto.
qs: Why can't Congress change the President's salary during a term?
What two purposes of the veto does Hamilton give?
Why does Hamilton think a qualified veto will be used more than an absolute one?

k.q: a power over a man's support is a power over his will
k.w: Why the salary cannot change during a term.

k.q: The propensity of the legislative department to intrude upon the rights, and to absorb the powers, of the other departments
k.w: Why the President needs a defense.

k.q: a salutary check upon the legislative body, calculated to guard the community against the effects of faction, precipitancy
k.w: The broader purpose of the veto.

papers.t: The Command of the Military and Naval Forces, and the Pardoning Power of the Executive
papers.s: Hamilton briefly defends the President's role as commander in chief, the power to ask cabinet officers for written opinions, and the pardon power, including for treason.
papers.c: Mason and others objected that the President could pardon people for treason, perhaps even accomplices of his own.
papers.m: War requires direction by one person. The power to require written opinions is a modest check. The pardon power should be held by one person, who will feel responsible for its use, and "humanity and good policy" call for it to be as free as possible. In rebellions, a timely pardon can restore peace.
qs: Why does Hamilton think a single person should hold the pardon power?
Mason objected to pardons for treason. What was his worry, and how does Hamilton answer?
What limits does the Constitution place on the pardon power (for example, impeachment)?

k.q: Of all the cares or concerns of government, the direction of war most peculiarly demands those qualities which distinguish the exercise of power by a single hand
k.w: Why one person commands.

k.q: Humanity and good policy conspire to dictate, that the benign prerogative of pardoning should be as little as possible fettered or embarrassed
k.w: His defense of the pardon power.

k.q: a well-timed offer of pardon to the insurgents or rebels may restore the tranquillity of the commonwealth
k.w: Why pardon for treason can be useful.

papers.t: The Treaty-Making Power of the Executive
papers.s: Hamilton defends treaty-making by the President with two-thirds of the Senate, arguing that the power is neither purely executive nor purely legislative.
papers.c: Jay had discussed treaties in No. 64. Critics wanted the House included, or a two-thirds vote of the whole Senate rather than of members present.
papers.m: Treaties are agreements with foreign nations, with the force of law, so the power fits neither branch alone. A President, serving four years, should not have it alone; nor should the Senate, which lacks secrecy and speed. Including the House would be impractical because it is large and changing. Requiring two-thirds of all senators, not just those present, would invite delay.
qs: Why does Hamilton say the treaty power belongs to neither branch alone?
Why is the House left out of treaties? Is that a good choice?
Compare this paper with Jay's No. 64.

k.q: the power of making treaties
k.w: Hamilton places it between the branches.

k.q: The history of human conduct does not warrant that exalted opinion of human virtue
k.w: Why the President should not make treaties alone.

papers.t: The Appointing Power of the Executive
papers.s: Hamilton defends presidential nomination of officers with Senate consent: one person will choose more carefully, and the Senate will check favoritism.
papers.c: New York's governor shared appointments with a Council of Appointment, which Hamilton thought invited intrigue.
papers.m: One person, solely responsible, will feel "a livelier sense of duty." A large body would trade favors. The Senate's consent is "an excellent check upon a spirit of favoritism" and will make the President ashamed to propose unfit candidates. Hamilton doubts the President could buy enough senators with offices to control them.
qs: What does Hamilton think is wrong with appointments made by a council or a large body?
How is the Senate's consent supposed to improve appointments?
Senate confirmations are often contested today. Does Hamilton's reasoning still hold? Give two views.

k.q: The sole and undivided responsibility of one man will naturally beget a livelier sense of duty
k.w: Why the President nominates.

k.q: an excellent check upon a spirit of favoritism in the President
k.w: Why the Senate consents.

papers.t: The Appointing Power Continued and Other Powers of the Executive Considered
papers.s: Hamilton finishes the executive papers, says the Senate's consent would be needed to remove officers as well as appoint them, and reviews the President's remaining duties.
papers.c: Whether the President can remove officers without the Senate became a major question. Congress debated it in 1789, and the Supreme Court has addressed it in cases such as Myers v. United States (1926). Scholars disagree about what Hamilton meant in this passage.
papers.m: Hamilton argues that requiring Senate consent brings stability, since a new President could not sweep out all officers at will. He answers the worry that the President and Senate would influence each other improperly. He reviews other powers: reporting to Congress, convening it, receiving ambassadors and faithfully executing the laws. He concludes that the executive combines energy with safety.
qs: What does Hamilton say about removing officers? Why do scholars disagree about this passage?
List the President's remaining powers in this paper.
Does Hamilton's view of the presidency balance "energy" with "safety"? Explain.

k.q: the consent of that body would be necessary to displace as well as to appoint
k.w: The removal passage, read in different ways by later courts and scholars.

k.q: We have now completed a survey of the structure and powers of the executive department
k.w: His summary of the executive papers.

papers.t: The Judiciary Department
papers.s: Hamilton's defense of judges who serve during good behavior, and the classic early argument for judicial review: courts must treat the Constitution as a higher law than ordinary statutes.
papers.c: Nos. 78 to 83 first appeared in the second volume of McLean's book edition on May 28, 1788, and were later reprinted in New York newspapers. Brutus had argued in a series of essays that the federal courts would become too powerful. The Supreme Court has quoted this paper many times; Marbury v. Madison (1803) adopted a similar line of reasoning.
papers.m: The judiciary is "the least dangerous" branch: it has neither the sword nor the purse, "neither FORCE nor WILL, but merely judgment." So it needs life tenure to stay independent. A limited constitution can only be kept through courts, which must declare acts contrary to it void. This does not make judges superior to the legislature; it means the will of the people, in the Constitution, is above both. Independent judges also protect individuals from unjust laws passed in moments of passion.
qs: Why does Hamilton call the judiciary "the least dangerous" branch? Do you agree today? Give arguments on each side.
Explain Hamilton's argument for judicial review in three steps.
Brutus XI to XV warned that federal judges would be beyond any control. Compare the two views.
Why does Hamilton think judges need permanent tenure?

k.q: the judiciary, from the nature of its functions, will always be the least dangerous to the political rights of the Constitution
k.w: Hamilton's famous claim about the courts.

k.q: It may truly be said to have neither FORCE nor WILL, but merely judgment
k.w: Why the courts are weak.

k.q: No legislative act, therefore, contrary to the Constitution, can be valid
k.w: The heart of judicial review.

k.q: The interpretation of the laws is the proper and peculiar province of the courts
k.w: A line later echoed by Chief Justice Marshall.

k.q: It only supposes that the power of the people is superior to both
k.w: Why review does not make judges supreme.

papers.t: The Judiciary Continued
papers.s: Hamilton defends fixed salaries for judges that cannot be cut, and explains that judges can be removed only by impeachment, not for old age or vague charges of inability.
papers.c: The Constitution says judges' pay cannot be reduced while they hold office. New York's constitution then retired judges at age 60, which Hamilton criticizes.
papers.m: "A power over a man's subsistence amounts to a power over his will." So judges' pay cannot be cut, though it can be raised as prices change. Judges answer for misconduct through impeachment. Hamilton argues against removing judges for "inability," which is hard to measure, and against a fixed retirement age, which would discard wise judges.
qs: Why can judges' salaries be raised but not cut?
Why does Hamilton oppose a retirement age for judges? Some states have one today. Give the reasons for each side.
How does this paper connect to No. 73 on the President's salary?

k.q: a power over a man's subsistence amounts to a power over his will
k.w: Why judges' pay is protected.

k.q: The precautions for their responsibility are comprised in the article respecting impeachments
k.w: How judges are held accountable.

papers.t: The Powers of the Judiciary
papers.s: Hamilton explains how far federal judicial power should reach: cases under the Constitution and federal laws, cases involving the nation, disputes between states and between citizens of different states, and maritime cases.
papers.c: Article III lists the kinds of cases federal courts may hear. Anti-Federalists feared these courts would swallow the state courts.
papers.m: Federal courts must have power over cases arising under federal law, so the Constitution can be enforced; otherwise thirteen courts with final say would be "a hydra in government." They should handle disputes between states, cases involving foreign nations, and cases between citizens of different states, where state courts might be partial. Hamilton goes clause by clause and finds each justified.
qs: What is "diversity jurisdiction" (cases between citizens of different states), and why did Hamilton think it was needed?
What does Hamilton mean by "a hydra in government"?
Which of the listed kinds of cases did Anti-Federalists worry about most? Why?

k.q: there ought always to be a constitutional method of giving efficacy to constitutional provisions
k.w: Why federal courts must enforce the Constitution.

k.q: Thirteen independent courts of final jurisdiction over the same causes, arising upon the same laws, is a hydra in government
k.w: Why one final court is needed.

k.q: It may be esteemed the basis of the Union
k.w: On the rights of citizens in every state.

papers.t: The Judiciary Continued, and the Distribution of the Judicial Authority
papers.s: Hamilton answers Brutus's warning that the Supreme Court would be uncontrollable, explains inferior courts and appellate review, and says states cannot be sued without their consent.
papers.c: Brutus argued that the Supreme Court, interpreting the Constitution by its "spirit," would be above every other power. Courts have cited Hamilton's line on state sovereign immunity in cases such as Hans v. Louisiana (1890) and Alden v. Maine (1999). The Eleventh Amendment (1795) addressed suits against states after Chisholm v. Georgia (1793).
papers.m: A separate supreme court is better than a legislature acting as final judge, as Britain's House of Lords did. Nothing in the plan lets courts follow the Constitution's "spirit" more than state courts can. If judges overreach, Congress can impeach and remove them. Congress may create lower courts. Appellate review of facts does not abolish juries. And states cannot be sued by individuals without their consent.
qs: What was Brutus's fear about the Supreme Court, and how does Hamilton answer it?
What check does Hamilton say Congress has over judges?
What is sovereign immunity? How did the Eleventh Amendment respond to Chisholm v. Georgia?

k.q: there is not a syllable in the plan under consideration which DIRECTLY empowers the national courts to construe the laws according to the spirit of the Constitution
k.w: Hamilton's answer to Brutus.

k.q: the supposed danger of judiciary encroachments on the legislative authority
k.w: Why he thinks courts will not take over.

k.q: It is inherent in the nature of sovereignty not to be amenable to the suit of an individual WITHOUT ITS CONSENT
k.w: The state sovereign immunity passage.

papers.t: The Judiciary Continued
papers.s: Hamilton explains how state and federal courts will share work: state courts keep their jurisdiction unless the Constitution takes it away, and appeals can go from state courts to the Supreme Court.
papers.c: A short paper on how the two court systems fit together. Courts have cited it on concurrent jurisdiction.
papers.m: A new government will raise questions only time can settle. State courts can hear many federal-law cases unless Congress gives them only to federal courts. The national and state systems are to be regarded as "ONE WHOLE," so appeals may go from state courts to the Supreme Court.
qs: What is concurrent jurisdiction?
Why does Hamilton think appeals from state courts to the Supreme Court are needed?

k.q: THE erection of a new government, whatever care or wisdom may distinguish the work, cannot fail to originate questions of intricacy and nicety
k.w: Hamilton admits not every question can be settled in advance.

k.q: the national and State systems are to be regarded as ONE WHOLE
k.w: How the court systems fit together.

papers.t: The Judiciary Continued in Relation to Trial by Jury
papers.s: Hamilton answers the most effective objection to the Constitution, that it does not guarantee jury trials in civil cases, arguing that silence does not abolish juries and that a single national rule would be hard to write.
papers.c: Article III guarantees jury trials in criminal cases but says nothing of civil cases. Anti-Federalists, including the Federal Farmer and Centinel, made this a leading complaint. The Seventh Amendment (1791) later guaranteed civil juries in federal suits at common law above twenty dollars.
papers.m: Hamilton says the Constitution's silence on civil juries does not abolish them; Congress may provide for them. Both sides value juries, but juries are more important against oppressive prosecutions than in civil suits. States differed so much in their civil jury practices that no single rule fit them all. The Massachusetts proposal would not have worked well.
qs: Why did the Constitution's silence on civil juries alarm Anti-Federalists?
What reasons does Hamilton give for not writing a civil jury rule into the Constitution?
How did the Seventh Amendment settle the question?

k.q: The rules of legal interpretation are rules of common sense
k.w: His reply to legal arguments that silence means abolition.

k.q: The friends and adversaries of the plan of the convention, if they agree in nothing else, concur at least in the value they set upon the trial by jury
k.w: Common ground between the sides.

k.q: the very palladium of free government
k.w: How opponents described jury trial.

papers.t: Certain General and Miscellaneous Objections to the Constitution Considered and Answered
papers.s: Hamilton answers the demand for a bill of rights: the Constitution already protects many rights, and listing others could be dangerous by implying powers that were never granted.
papers.c: The lack of a bill of rights was the Anti-Federalists' most powerful argument. Several states ratified while recommending amendments. In 1789 Madison proposed amendments in the First Congress, and the Bill of Rights was ratified in 1791. The Ninth Amendment answers the worry Hamilton raises here.
papers.m: The Constitution already protects habeas corpus, bans bills of attainder, ex post facto laws and titles of nobility, and guarantees jury trial in criminal cases. Bills of rights began as limits on kings; here the people grant only limited powers and "surrender nothing." Listing rights would be dangerous: "why declare that things shall not be done which there is no power to do?" It could give a pretext to claim more power. The Constitution itself, he concludes, is a bill of rights. He also answers objections about the distance of the capital and cost.
qs: List the rights Hamilton says the Constitution already protects.
Why does Hamilton think a bill of rights could be dangerous? How does the Ninth Amendment answer his worry?
Read the Federal Farmer IV or Brutus II (summary). Why did Anti-Federalists think a bill of rights was essential?
Who turned out to be right about the need for a bill of rights? Explain how both sides could claim part of the outcome.

k.q: bills of rights are, in their origin, stipulations between kings and their subjects
k.w: Why Hamilton thinks America is different.

k.q: Here, in strictness, the people surrender nothing
k.w: Powers are delegated, not surrendered.

k.q: For why declare that things shall not be done which there is no power to do?
k.w: The core of his argument.

k.q: the Constitution is itself, in every rational sense, and to every useful purpose, A BILL OF RIGHTS
k.w: His conclusion.

papers.t: Concluding Remarks
papers.s: Hamilton concludes the series: the plan is not perfect but is the best that can be had; it should be adopted now, and amended afterward if needed.
papers.c: By the time this paper appeared in book form (May 28, 1788), eight states had ratified. New York's convention would open in June. Many opponents wanted amendments before ratification.
papers.m: Hamilton reviews the series and says the Constitution resembles New York's own. He grants that it has flaws: "I never expect to see a perfect work from imperfect man." Holding out for amendments first would mean a second convention and new compromises among thirteen states. After adoption, amendments could be made one at a time; in his words, "whenever nine, or rather ten States, were united in the desire of a particular amendment," it would pass. He warns that "a nation, without a national government, is, in my view, an awful spectacle."
qs: Why does Hamilton think it is easier to amend the Constitution after adoption than before?
The Plebeian argued the opposite: amend first. Compare their arguments.
What happened next? Use the ratification timeline to see how New York decided.

k.q: I never expect to see a perfect work from imperfect man
k.w: Hamilton's humility about the plan.

k.q: every amendment to the Constitution, if once established, would be a single proposition
k.w: Why amending later is easier.

k.q: A NATION, without a NATIONAL GOVERNMENT, is, in my view, an awful spectacle
k.w: The stakes, at the end.
